title: Early Wittgenstein: The Limits of Language
subtitle: A book written in the trenches that tried to draw the border of everything that can be said
objectives: By the end you will be able to tell the story of the young Wittgenstein, from engineering student to soldier to village schoolteacher
Explain the picture theory of meaning and how the Tractatus thinks language connects to the world
Explain the distinction between what can be said and what can only be shown
Interpret the famous final proposition and the image of the ladder that must be thrown away
Compare the 'ineffable' and 'resolute' readings of the Tractatus and judge which makes more sense
hook:
Cambridge, autumn 1911. An intense young Austrian engineer, who has been designing aircraft propellers in Manchester, turns up unannounced at Bertrand Russell's rooms and starts arguing with him about logic. He keeps coming back, often staying late into the night, pacing up and down. Russell is not sure whether he is a genius or a crank. At the end of the term the young man asks him directly: is he a complete idiot? If so, he will become an aeronaut; if not, a philosopher. Russell tells him to write something over the vacation. When he brings it back, Russell, by his own account, read only one sentence before telling him that he must on no account become an aeronaut.

The young man was Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951), and within a few years Russell would feel that his pupil had surpassed him. The book Wittgenstein wrote, much of it in notebooks carried through the First World War, is one of the strangest and most influential works of philosophy ever written: the *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus*. It is barely seventy-five pages long. It claims to have solved, in essentials, all the problems of philosophy. And it ends by telling you that almost everything it has just said is, strictly speaking, nonsense. Today we try to understand why.

sections.heading: A Life of Extremes
sections.body:
Wittgenstein was born in Vienna in 1889, the youngest of eight children of Karl Wittgenstein, a steel magnate and one of the richest men in the Habsburg Empire. The family palace was a center of Viennese culture; Brahms and Mahler were visitors. His brother Paul became a concert pianist, lost his right arm in the First World War, and commissioned works for the left hand alone, most famously Ravel's Piano Concerto for the Left Hand. But the family was also deeply troubled. Three of Ludwig's four brothers died by suicide, and he himself struggled with thoughts of suicide for much of his life.

He studied engineering in Berlin and then aeronautics in Manchester, where his interest in the mathematics of propellers led him to the foundations of mathematics, then to Russell's work, and then to Frege (Day 69). He visited Frege in Jena, and Frege advised him to study with Russell in Cambridge.

At Cambridge he worked ferociously. Russell later described him as perhaps the most perfect example he had known of genius as traditionally conceived: passionate, profound, intense and dominating. In 1913 Wittgenstein withdrew to a hut he had built in a remote fjord at Skjolden in Norway to think about logic in solitude.

When war broke out in 1914 he volunteered for the Austro-Hungarian army, although a hernia would have exempted him. He served on a gunboat, in artillery, and as an observer on the Eastern and later the Italian front, deliberately seeking the most dangerous posts and winning decorations for bravery. In a bookshop in Galicia he found Tolstoy's *The Gospel in Brief* and carried it everywhere, so constantly that fellow soldiers knew him as "the man with the gospels." Throughout, he kept philosophical notebooks. The *Tractatus* was finished in 1918, shortly before he was captured by the Italians. From a prisoner-of-war camp near Monte Cassino he managed, with the help of the economist John Maynard Keynes, to get the manuscript to Russell.

The book was published in German in 1921 and in an English translation, with an introduction by Russell, in 1922. Wittgenstein disliked the introduction and felt even Russell had not understood him. Remember that pattern: few people have ever been confident they understood the *Tractatus*.

sections.heading: The World Is Everything That Is the Case
sections.body:
The *Tractatus* looks like no other philosophy book. It consists of short numbered remarks. There are seven main propositions, numbered 1 to 7, and the decimal numbers show how other remarks comment on them: 2.1 comments on 2, 2.11 on 2.1, and so on. It reads less like an argument than like a set of crystal-hard pronouncements.

It opens: "The world is everything that is the case." And then: "The world is the totality of facts, not of things." (1 and 1.1.)

Why facts rather than things? A list of things (a cat, a mat, a window) does not tell you what the world is like. The world is the cat being *on* the mat, the window being open. What exists are things *arranged* in certain ways, and an arrangement is a fact.

Wittgenstein, building on Russell's logical atomism (Day 69), argues that complex facts break down into **atomic facts** (he calls them states of affairs): the simplest possible combinations of the simplest possible things, which he calls **objects**. Atomic facts are independent of one another: any one could obtain or fail to obtain without affecting the others. The world is the sum of which atomic facts obtain.

What exactly are these simple objects? Wittgenstein never gave a single example. He seems to have thought that logic requires that there be such simples, whatever they turn out to be. That frustrating silence is itself typical of the book: it describes the logical form any world must have, not what is actually in this one.

sections.heading: The Picture Theory of Meaning
sections.body:
How does language connect to such a world? According to a story Wittgenstein later told a friend, the key idea came to him during the war when he read about a court case in Paris in which a traffic accident was represented in the courtroom using a model with toy cars and dolls. The model could show how the accident happened because each toy stood for a real thing, and the arrangement of the toys stood for the arrangement of the real things.

That is the **picture theory of meaning**. "A proposition is a picture of reality," Wittgenstein writes (4.01). A meaningful sentence is a logical picture of a possible fact. Its simple parts, names, stand for simple objects, and the way the names are combined depicts a way the objects might be combined. If the objects really are combined that way, the sentence is true; if not, false.

This explains a remarkable thing: you can understand a sentence you have never heard before, such as "There is a blue giraffe in the library." You do not need anyone to tell you what it means, because you know what its parts stand for and how they are arranged. And you understand it without knowing whether it is true. A picture can be false and still be a picture.

For a picture to depict reality, it must share something with reality: its **logical form**, the structure of possible combinations. A map shares the spatial arrangement of the land it maps; a musical score shares a structure with the sound of the performance. Every meaningful sentence shares logical form with the possible fact it depicts.

Complex sentences are built from simple ones by logical connectives such as "and," "or" and "not." Their truth depends only on the truth of their parts, which the *Tractatus* shows by the method of **truth tables**, still taught in every introductory logic class. Some combinations come out true no matter what: these are **tautologies**, the truths of logic. "It is raining or it is not raining" is always true, but, as Wittgenstein points out (4.461), knowing it tells you nothing about the weather. Logical truths say nothing about the world; they show its form.

sections.heading: What Can Be Said and What Can Only Be Shown
sections.body:
Now comes the twist. If meaningful language consists of pictures of possible facts, then a great deal that we try to say turns out to be unsayable.

First, logical form itself cannot be pictured. A picture cannot depict its own form of depiction, just as you cannot draw a map that depicts the relationship of mapping. Logical form **shows** itself in meaningful sentences, but it cannot be **said**. "What can be shown, cannot be said" (4.1212).

Second, and more strikingly, ethics, aesthetics and religion fall outside the limits of language. Facts are just facts: one thing happening rather than another. Values are not further facts in the world. If there were value in the world, Wittgenstein argues, it would be just one more fact, and so it would have no value. The sense of the world must lie outside the world (6.41). Therefore ethics cannot be put into words (6.421). This is not because ethics is unimportant. On the contrary, it is because ethics is too important to be one more item on the list of facts.

Third, there is what Wittgenstein calls **the mystical**: "It is not how things are in the world that is mystical, but that it exists" (6.44). He also writes that even when all possible scientific questions have been answered, the problems of life remain completely untouched (6.52).

And fourth, the self. The thinking subject is not an object in the world but a limit of the world, like the eye that sees but never appears in its own field of vision (5.633). "The limits of my language mean the limits of my world" (5.6).

In a 1919 letter to a publisher, Ludwig von Ficker, Wittgenstein explained that his work consisted of two parts: what was written in the book, and everything he had *not* written. The second part, he said, was the important one. The book draws a border around what can be said from the inside, so that what lies outside, ethics and the meaning of life, is protected by silence.

sections.heading: Whereof One Cannot Speak: The Ladder and the Silence
sections.body:
Here we reach the most famous paradox in the book. The *Tractatus* itself is full of sentences about logical form, the relation between language and world, the self and ethics. By its own theory, these sentences do not picture any possible facts. So they are not meaningful.

Wittgenstein faces this head-on, near the very end: his propositions serve as elucidations, in that whoever understands him eventually recognizes them as nonsensical, when he has used them to climb beyond them. He must, so to speak, throw away the ladder after he has climbed up it (6.54). Then he must transcend these propositions, and he will see the world aright.

And then the final proposition, all by itself: "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent" (7, in C.K. Ogden's 1922 translation; the later translation by David Pears and Brian McGuinness renders it "What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence").

What does this mean for philosophy? The *Tractatus* says that the right method would be to say nothing except what can be said, that is, the propositions of natural science, and whenever someone wanted to say something metaphysical, to show him that he had given no meaning to certain signs in his sentences (6.53). Philosophy is not a body of doctrine but an activity of clarification.

In the preface Wittgenstein claimed that the truth of the thoughts in the book seemed to him unassailable and definitive, and that he believed he had found, in essentials, the final solution of the problems. But he added that the book also shows how little is achieved when these problems are solved.

sections.heading: After the Tractatus, and How to Read It
sections.body:
Wittgenstein took his conclusion seriously. If philosophy was finished, he would do something else. He gave away his enormous inheritance to his siblings and from 1920 to 1926 taught at elementary schools in poor villages in rural Lower Austria. He was a dedicated but harsh and demanding teacher. In 1926, after he struck a pupil who collapsed, he faced a legal hearing and left teaching; years later he went back to apologize to the villagers. He then worked briefly as a monastery gardener's assistant and spent two years designing a starkly beautiful house in Vienna for his sister Margarethe, obsessing over the exact height of the ceilings and the design of the door handles.

Meanwhile the *Tractatus* had found eager readers in Vienna. A group of scientifically minded philosophers, the Vienna Circle, read it line by line and saw in it a weapon against metaphysics. Tomorrow (Day 71) we will see how they used it, and how they misunderstood its respect for the mystical. In 1929 Wittgenstein returned to Cambridge and submitted the *Tractatus* as his doctoral thesis. The story goes that at the end of the oral examination he clapped his examiners, Russell and Moore, on the shoulder and told them not to worry, because he knew they would never understand it. Then he began to tear his own masterpiece apart, as Day 73 explains.

How should we read the book? Scholars divide into two broad camps.

- The **traditional** or "ineffabilist" reading holds that Wittgenstein believed there are deep truths, about logical form, ethics and the mystical, that cannot be said but can be shown. The book gestures at them through nonsense that is somehow illuminating.
- The **resolute** reading, developed since the 1980s by Cora Diamond and James Conant, takes the ladder passage at its word: the nonsense is plain nonsense, and there are no secret unsayable truths. The book is a kind of therapy that leads the reader to see through the temptation to say such things at all.

Both readings face difficulties. The first seems to say what it claims cannot be said. The second has to explain why Wittgenstein wrote so passionately about the importance of what lies beyond language. Either way, the book poses a question that never goes away: are there things that matter deeply but cannot be put into words?

keyQuote.text: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
keyQuote.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921), proposition 5.6 (trans. C.K. Ogden)

modernConnection.title: The World as a Database, and What It Leaves Out
modernConnection.body:
The *Tractatus* pictures the world as a vast collection of independent facts, each of which either obtains or does not, and language as a system for recording them. That picture would describe a modern database remarkably well. Knowledge graphs used by search engines store the world as millions of simple statements of the form "thing, relation, thing": Paris is the capital of France; Venus is a planet. Digital twins, detailed computer models of factories, cities or even human hearts, try to mirror every relevant fact about a real system so that engineers can test changes on the model first, rather like the toy cars in that Paris courtroom.

Our age is also tempted by the *Tractatus*'s view of what counts as meaningful. In many organizations, what cannot be measured hardly exists: performance dashboards, metrics and key performance indicators record facts, and anything that does not fit becomes invisible. Wittgenstein would recognize the boundary being drawn. But he would draw the opposite moral. For him, the things that cannot be stated as facts, such as the value of a life, the meaning of one's work, the beauty of a piece of music, are not unimportant; they are the most important things of all. A hospital that tracks waiting times but cannot record kindness, or a school that measures test scores but not curiosity, has made a Tractarian mistake in reverse: it has treated what lies outside its language as if it did not matter.

The comparison also has limits. Real databases are messy, constantly revised and full of vague categories, and modern AI language models do not work like the picture theory at all: they learn statistical patterns of word use rather than mapping names to objects. Wittgenstein himself came to reject the picture theory for reasons that sound very like that, as Day 73 will show. But the question he raised, what our systems of representation inevitably leave out, has never been more urgent.

vocabulary.definition: Wittgenstein's only philosophical book published in his lifetime (1921), a sequence of numbered remarks on logic, language, the world and the limits of what can be said.
vocabulary.example: The Tractatus opens with 'The world is everything that is the case.'

vocabulary.definition: The Tractatus view that a meaningful proposition is a logical picture of a possible fact, whose elements stand for objects and whose arrangement depicts their arrangement.
vocabulary.example: According to the picture theory, 'the cup is on the table' is meaningful because its structure mirrors a possible arrangement of cup and table.

vocabulary.definition: In the Tractatus, the simplest kind of fact, a combination of simple objects that is logically independent of all other atomic facts.
vocabulary.example: Wittgenstein never gave an example of an atomic fact, insisting only that logic requires them.

vocabulary.definition: The structure of possibility that a picture must share with what it depicts in order to represent it at all.
vocabulary.example: A musical score and a performance share a logical form, which is why one can be read off from the other.

vocabulary.definition: A proposition that is true whatever the facts are, and so says nothing about the world, such as 'It is raining or it is not raining.'
vocabulary.example: Wittgenstein argued that the truths of logic are tautologies that show the form of the world without describing it.

vocabulary.definition: The Tractatus distinction between what can be stated in meaningful propositions (facts) and what can only reveal itself (logical form, and perhaps ethics and the mystical).
vocabulary.example: By the distinction between saying and showing, the logical form of a sentence is displayed in it but cannot be described by it.

vocabulary.definition: Wittgenstein's term for what lies beyond the limits of language, especially the wonder that the world exists at all.
vocabulary.example: For the early Wittgenstein, the mystical is not how the world is but that it is.

vocabulary.definition: An interpretation of the Tractatus holding that its self-described nonsense is simply nonsense, not a gesture toward hidden ineffable truths.
vocabulary.example: On the resolute reading, throwing away the ladder means abandoning the urge to state deep metaphysical truths at all.

thinkingExercise.title: Drawing the Limits of Your Language
thinkingExercise.prompt: Test the Tractatus's boundary between the sayable and the unsayable on your own life. Spend 10 to 15 minutes writing.
steps: Write five sentences that state plain facts you could in principle check (for example, about your street, your body or the weather). Note how each could be true or false.

Now try to write one sentence stating the most important thing in your life, or what makes your life meaningful. Is it a fact like the first five? Could it be checked? If not, what kind of statement is it?
Think of something important you have shown someone rather than said: through an action, a gift, a look, a piece of music. Why might showing have worked better than saying?
Consider the claim that 'ethics cannot be put into words.' Write a reply arguing that ethical statements are meaningful after all, then a short response Wittgenstein might give.
Reflect: do you lean toward the traditional reading (there are deep truths that can only be shown) or the resolute reading (there is nothing there to say)? Why?

summary: Wittgenstein, a wealthy, intense Viennese engineer turned Russell's student, wrote the Tractatus largely while serving as a soldier in the First World War.
The Tractatus holds that the world is the totality of facts, ultimately atomic facts composed of simple objects.
According to the picture theory, a meaningful proposition is a logical picture of a possible fact, sharing its logical form; truths of logic are tautologies that say nothing about the world.

Logical form, ethics, aesthetics, the self and the mystical cannot be said but only shown; the book's own propositions are a ladder to be thrown away, ending with 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.'
Believing he had solved philosophy, Wittgenstein left it to teach school, before returning to Cambridge in 1929; scholars still debate between traditional and resolute readings of the book.

quiz.question: According to the opening of the Tractatus, what is the world made of?
options: Things
Ideas in the mind of God
Facts
Sense impressions
quiz.explanation: 'The world is the totality of facts, not of things' (1.1): things arranged in certain ways.

quiz.question: What inspired the picture theory, according to a story Wittgenstein later told?
options: A model of a traffic accident with toy cars and dolls used in a Paris court case
A painting he saw in a Viennese museum
Plato's Allegory of the Cave
A photograph of the battlefield
quiz.explanation: The courtroom model showed how arranged elements standing for real things can depict a possible state of affairs.

quiz.question: According to the picture theory, a sentence can be meaningful even if it is false.
quiz.explanation: A proposition pictures a possible fact; it is meaningful whether or not that fact obtains, just as a model can depict an accident that did not happen.

quiz.question: Why does 'Either it is raining or it is not raining' tell you nothing about the weather, according to the Tractatus?
options: Because weather statements are meaningless
Because it is a contradiction
Because it pictures an atomic fact
Because it is a tautology, true whatever the facts are
quiz.explanation: Tautologies hold in every possible situation, so they rule nothing out and say nothing about the world (4.461).

quiz.question: Why, according to the Tractatus, can ethics not be put into words?
options: Because ethics is unimportant
Because value is not a fact in the world, and meaningful sentences only picture facts
Because ethical rules are too complicated
Because only God can speak about ethics
quiz.explanation: If value were in the world it would be just another fact; the sense of the world lies outside it. Wittgenstein thought ethics was supremely important.

quiz.question: Wittgenstein's letter to Ludwig von Ficker said that the most important part of his book was the part he did not write.
quiz.explanation: He described the work as having two parts, what was written and what was not, and said the unwritten part was the important one.

quiz.question: What does Wittgenstein mean by saying the reader must 'throw away the ladder'?
options: Philosophy should be abandoned in favor of engineering
Russell's logic is useless
The book's own propositions, once used to see the world aright, must be recognized as nonsense
Readers should skip the difficult parts of the book
quiz.explanation: By its own theory, the Tractatus's propositions do not picture facts, so they are nonsense, though they can help the reader climb to a clear view (6.54).

quiz.question: A company evaluates staff only by measurable output and ignores kindness and integrity because they don't appear on dashboards. Which Tractatus idea does this most usefully illuminate, by contrast?
options: That the most important things may lie outside what can be stated as facts
That logic consists of tautologies
That atomic facts are independent of one another
That the world is made of things, not facts
quiz.explanation: Wittgenstein held that value cannot be stated as a fact, yet is the most important thing; the dashboard treats what lies outside its language as if it did not matter.

quiz.question: After finishing the Tractatus, Wittgenstein immediately took up a professorship and continued publishing philosophy throughout the 1920s.
quiz.explanation: He gave away his fortune and taught elementary school in rural Austria, believing philosophy's problems had been solved, and only returned to Cambridge in 1929.

quiz.question: What distinguishes the 'resolute' reading of the Tractatus from the traditional one?
options: It holds that the Tractatus was written by Russell
It claims the book's nonsense secretly conveys ineffable truths
It treats the picture theory as literally about painting
It holds that the book's nonsense is plain nonsense with no hidden truths behind it
quiz.explanation: Diamond and Conant argue the book works as therapy, freeing us from the urge to say such things, rather than gesturing at unsayable truths.

goDeeper.body:
The ethical side of the *Tractatus* is easy to overlook, but Wittgenstein's 'Lecture on Ethics,' given in Cambridge in 1929, makes it vivid. He describes experiences like wondering at the existence of the world and feeling absolutely safe whatever happens, and argues that every attempt to express them produces nonsense, because they try to go beyond the world and significant language. Yet he ends by saying he would not for his life ridicule this tendency in the human mind; he personally deeply respects it. This lecture is the best evidence for the traditional reading, and resolute readers must explain it.

A second debate concerns the book's relation to Schopenhauer (Day 60). Wittgenstein read *The World as Will and Representation* as a teenager, and remarks on the self as the limit of the world, on the will as the bearer of good and evil, and on living in the present (6.4311: eternal life belongs to those who live in the present) carry Schopenhauerian and Tolstoyan echoes. Some scholars see the *Tractatus* as a fusion of Frege and Russell's logic with Schopenhauer's mysticism, a combination that baffled both the logicians and the mystics.

Finally, consider the influence of Frank Ramsey, the brilliant Cambridge mathematician who helped translate the *Tractatus* at nineteen, visited Wittgenstein in his Austrian village in 1923 to discuss it, and later pressed objections, for example about whether atomic propositions are really independent of each other ('this is red' seems to exclude 'this is green'). Wittgenstein himself came to see this 'color exclusion' problem as a crack in the system. Ramsey, who died at twenty-six in 1930, was also an admirer of the pragmatists (Day 67), and pragmatist ideas may have reached the later Wittgenstein partly through him. Cheryl Misak's biography of Ramsey tells this story.

readings.title: Ludwig Wittgenstein: The Duty of Genius
readings.author: Ray Monk
readings.note: The definitive, gripping biography; chapters 6–9 cover the war, the Tractatus and the village years.

readings.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
readings.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein (trans. D.F. Pears and B.F. McGuinness)
readings.note: Read the preface and the 6s and 7 first; then dip into the 1s, 2s and 4s.

readings.title: Wittgenstein's Vienna
readings.author: Allan Janik and Stephen Toulmin
readings.note: Places the Tractatus in the cultural crisis of fin-de-siècle Vienna and argues for its ethical purpose.

readings.title: Frank Ramsey: A Sheer Excess of Powers
readings.author: Cheryl Misak
readings.note: Biography of Wittgenstein's young critic and translator, linking Cambridge to pragmatism.

questions: Can there be truths that cannot be put into words? If so, how could anyone know them?
Is the Tractatus self-refuting, or does the image of the ladder rescue it?
Does 'the limits of my language mean the limits of my world' imply that learning new languages or vocabularies can literally enlarge your world?
